title: Design a News Feed
summary: Build a social feed that handles both friends and celebrities. Start with posts and follows, compare fan-out on write and read, combine them in a hybrid, then add feed caches, cursor pagination and ranking.
body:
## Practice first

Design the home feed of a social network such as Facebook or Twitter/X: users publish posts, follow other users, and open the app to a scrolling feed of recent posts from the accounts they follow. Most accounts have a few hundred followers; a handful have over 100 million.

Spend 10 minutes on a sketch first: requirements, entities, the three endpoints and a baseline that returns the right feed. Mark where that baseline breaks as traffic grows. Then compare your choices with this design; there is more than one defensible answer.

## Functional requirements

Core (users should be able to):

1. **Create a post** with text and optional media.
2. **Follow and unfollow** other users (one-directional, no approval needed).
3. **View a home feed** of posts from accounts they follow, newest first, with infinite scroll.

Out of scope: likes and comments (we only display counts), ads, search, notifications, direct messages, and a full machine-learned ranking system (we discuss ranking briefly at the end). Media upload uses the standard blob pattern and is not designed here.

## Non-functional requirements

- **Scale:** 500M daily active users, 100M new posts per day, average 200 followees per user, some accounts with 100M+ followers.
- **Feed latency:** p99 under 300 ms for the first page, since it is the first screen of the app.
- **Availability over consistency for the feed:** a new post may take up to ~10 seconds to appear in followers' feeds. Authors get read-your-writes on their own posts (they see the post immediately).
- **Durability:** posts and follow edges are never lost; the feed itself is a derived, rebuildable cache.
- **Read-heavy:** feed reads outnumber posts by roughly 50 to 1.

## Back-of-the-envelope

- **Writes:** 100M posts / 86,400 s ≈ 1,200 posts/s average, maybe 5,000/s at peak. Easy for a sharded post store.
- **Reads:** 500M users × 10 feed loads/day = 5B/day ≈ 58,000 feed requests/s average, ~150,000/s peak. Each naive feed request would read follow lists and recent posts from ~200 authors. That is ~30M author lookups per second at peak, which is why **we cannot assemble feeds from scratch on every read**.
- **Fan-out on write cost:** 100M posts × 200 followers = 20B feed insertions/day ≈ 230,000/s. Large but parallelisable. The problem is the tail: one post by an account with 100M followers is 100M insertions on its own, minutes of work even at 1M inserts/s, and several celebrities posting during a live event multiply that. This is the number that forces a **hybrid** design.
- **Feed cache size:** keep the latest 500 post ids per user (8-byte ids plus overhead, call it ~16 KB per user in a compact encoding). For 300M users active in the last month that is ~5 TB of RAM, spread over a cluster of a few hundred cache nodes. Materialising feeds for all 2B+ registered users would be wasteful, so **only active users get a precomputed feed**; inactive users' feeds are rebuilt on demand.

## Core entities

- **User**: id, profile, follower count, a flag for "high fan-out" accounts.
- **Post**: post id (time-sortable, for example a Snowflake-style 64-bit id), author id, text, media references, created at, deleted flag.
- **Follow**: follower id, followee id, created at. Stored twice: by follower ("who do I follow") and by followee ("who follows me").
- **Feed entry**: user id, post id, author id. A derived, capped list per user.

```mermaid
erDiagram
    USER ||--o{ POST : writes
    USER ||--o{ FOLLOW : "follows (as follower)"
    USER ||--o{ FOLLOW : "followed by (as followee)"
    USER ||--o{ FEED_ENTRY : "has in feed"
    POST ||--o{ FEED_ENTRY : "appears as"
```

Keep the feed entry small: this derived, denormalised record holds only IDs. Fetch post text, media and counts when rendering the page, so an edit or deletion does not require rewriting millions of feed entries.

## API

All endpoints require an authenticated user; the user id comes from the token, not the request body.

```text
POST /v1/posts
Idempotency-Key: 5d1c...
{ "text": "Launch day!", "mediaIds": ["m_31"] }
-> 201 { "postId": "1849223371902713856", "createdAt": "..." }

POST   /v1/users/{userId}/followers      (follow userId)   -> 204
DELETE /v1/users/{userId}/followers/me   (unfollow)        -> 204

GET /v1/feed?limit=20&cursor=eyJwIjoxODQ5...
-> 200 {
  "items": [ { "postId": "...", "author": { "id": "...", "name": "..." },
               "text": "...", "media": [...], "likeCount": 12, "createdAt": "..." } ],
  "nextCursor": "eyJwIjoxODQ4..."
}
```

Pagination uses an opaque cursor encoding the last post id seen (and, for ranked feeds, a session snapshot id), never `offset`: new posts arrive at the top while a user scrolls, and offsets would show duplicates or skip posts.

## High-level design

**Create a post.** The post service writes the post to the post store, sharded by post id (or by author id if "all posts by author" is the dominant query; we keep an author-to-posts index either way), and returns 201.

**Follow.** The follow service writes both directions of the edge to the follow store, sharded by the leading user id of each table.

**View feed, naive version.** The feed service reads the user's followees, fetches each followee's latest posts, merges by time and returns the top 20. This is fan-out on read. It is correct and simple and works for a small product, but each request touches hundreds of shards (the 30M lookups/s computed above).

**View feed, baseline at scale.** On every new post, the post service publishes an event to a queue; **fan-out workers** read the author's follower list in pages and prepend the post id to each follower's **feed cache** (a capped list in Redis or a similar in-memory store). Reading a feed becomes one cache read plus hydration.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U["Client"] --> GW["API gateway"]
    GW --> PS["Post service"]
    GW --> FS["Follow service"]
    GW --> FD["Feed service"]
    PS --> PDB[("Post store")]
    PS --> Q[["Post events"]]
    FS --> FDB[("Follow store")]
    Q --> FW["Fan-out workers"]
    FW --> FDB
    FW --> FC[("Feed cache")]
    FD --> FC
    FD --> PC[("Post and user cache")]
    PC --> PDB
```

Walk through it. Dana posts. The post service stores the post (id `1849...`), publishes `PostCreated(dana, 1849...)` and returns. A fan-out worker pages through Dana's 300 followers and pushes `1849...` onto each follower's feed list, trimming each to 500 entries. A few seconds later Eli opens the app; the feed service reads the first 20 ids from Eli's list, multi-gets the posts and authors from the post cache, drops anything deleted or blocked, and returns the page with a cursor pointing at the last id.

## Deep dives

### 1. Fan-out on write, on read, or both (latency vs write amplification)

**Problem:** we want reads to be one cache lookup, but pushing a celebrity's post into 100M lists is slow and expensive, and most of those followers will not open the app before the post is buried.

- **Bad: pure fan-out on read.** Cheap writes, but every feed load touches ~200 authors' shards; p99 latency suffers and the post store takes all the read load.
- **Good: pure fan-out on write.** Fast reads, but write amplification is unbounded: a 100M-follower post creates a multi-minute backlog that delays every other post's delivery, and inactive followers' lists are updated for nothing.
- **Great: hybrid.** Fan out on write for normal authors (below a threshold, say 100k followers, or based on measured fan-out cost). Mark high-fan-out authors and skip their fan-out. At read time, the feed service merges the user's precomputed list with the recent posts of the few celebrities they follow (most users follow a handful at most), which are served from a hot, heavily replicated cache. Skip fan-out for followers who have not been active in 30 days too; their feeds are built on read if they return.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P["New post event"] --> C{"Author above follower threshold?"}
    C -->|No| W["Fan-out workers push id to active followers"]
    W --> FC[("Per-user feed cache")]
    C -->|Yes| H[("Celebrity recent-posts cache")]
    R["Feed request"] --> FC
    R --> H
    FC --> M["Merge by score, take page"]
    H --> M
    M --> OUT["Hydrated page"]
```

Normal posts are pushed into followers' feed lists ahead of time. Celebrity posts are written once to a small, replicated cache of each celebrity's recent posts. A feed request reads the user's list and the recent posts of the celebrities they follow, merges them, and hydrates the top of the merged list. The threshold is tunable: the merge cost on read grows with the number of celebrity followees, so it should stay small.

### 2. The read path: hydration and cursor pagination (feed latency)

**Problem:** a 300 ms p99 includes reading ids, fetching 20 posts and their authors, filtering, and serialising, across several services.

- **Bad: store full post objects in every feed list.** Reads are one hop, but an edit or delete has to rewrite millions of lists, and memory use grows by 50x.
- **Good: ids in the feed, multi-get hydration from a post cache.** Post and user objects are cached by id with a high hit rate because recent posts are shared across many feeds.
- **Great: ids plus parallel batched hydration, with filtering and over-fetch.** Read ~30 ids for a page of 20 so filtered items (deleted posts, blocked authors, unfollowed accounts) do not leave the page short; issue one multi-get per cache shard in parallel; keep counts (likes, replies) in a separate counter cache so a hot post's counter updates do not invalidate its body.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant F as Feed service
    participant FC as Feed cache
    participant HC as Celebrity cache
    participant PC as Post cache
    C->>F: GET feed, cursor after id 1849
    F->>FC: ids older than 1849, limit 30
    F->>HC: recent posts of 3 followed celebrities
    FC-->>F: 30 ids
    HC-->>F: 6 ids
    F->>F: merge, take 30 newest
    F->>PC: multi-get posts and authors
    PC-->>F: objects
    F->>F: drop deleted and blocked, keep 20
    F-->>C: 20 items, next cursor
```

The cursor encodes the last id returned, so the next request asks for ids strictly older than it; posts arriving at the top in the meantime cannot shift the page. The two cache reads happen in parallel. A cache miss on the feed list (inactive user, evicted entry, cache node lost) falls back to the fan-out-on-read path for that user and repopulates the list asynchronously, so the cache is an optimisation, never the source of truth.

### 3. Keeping fan-out healthy under bursts (freshness target)

The ~10 second freshness goal is a queue-lag SLO. Partition post events by author so each author's posts stay ordered, page through follower lists in chunks of a few thousand, and run fan-out workers that can scale out on lag. Prioritise: a burst of normal posts should not wait behind one borderline-celebrity's 90k-follower fan-out, so large fan-outs go to a separate lower-priority queue. Writes to the feed cache are pipelined per cache shard. If the cache cluster is degraded, workers apply backpressure and the read path's fallback (merge on read) keeps feeds correct, just slower.

Expect post events to be delivered again. Make feed updates idempotent by using post IDs as sorted-set members, or deduplicate on read, so replaying an event does not show the same post twice.

### 4. Follows, unfollows, deletes and privacy (correctness of a derived cache)

A precomputed feed goes stale whenever the inputs change:

- **New follow:** the new followee's recent posts are missing from the feed. Either backfill a handful of recent posts asynchronously, or let the read-time merge pull them in for a short window.
- **Unfollow or block:** do not scan and rewrite lists; filter at read time against the user's current follow and block sets (cached), and let old entries age out of the capped list.
- **Delete or privacy change:** the post cache marks the post deleted or restricted; hydration drops it. Feed lists are never the authority on visibility.

The feed cache is a shortlist, not a permission slip. Every read checks its candidates against authoritative visibility data. That check is what makes delayed fan-out safe.

### 5. Ranking, briefly

Modern feeds are not purely chronological. A practical structure: **candidate generation** (the fan-out list, celebrity posts, maybe suggested posts) → **lightweight scoring** (recency, affinity with the author, engagement so far, content type) → **page assembly** with diversity rules (no five posts in a row from one author). Ranking makes the "older than id X" cursor meaningless, because order is no longer by id; instead, rank a candidate set once per session, store the ranked list for that session briefly, and page through it with a cursor holding the session id and position. Keep a chronological fallback for when the ranker is slow or down.

## What interviewers look for

- **Mid-level:** a correct baseline with clean entities and API, recognises that assembling the feed on every read is expensive, proposes a feed cache with fan-out on write, and uses cursor pagination.
- **Senior:** quantifies fan-out, identifies the celebrity problem and proposes the hybrid with a clear threshold, stores ids rather than objects, explains hydration and read-time filtering, and treats the feed as a rebuildable cache with a fallback.
- **Staff:** discusses active-user-only materialisation and its memory cost, queue-lag SLOs and priority for fan-out, the consistency semantics of follows/unfollows/deletes, multi-region replication of feed caches, and how ranking changes pagination and caching.

## Common mistakes

- Offset pagination on a feed that changes while the user scrolls.
- Pure fan-out on write with no plan for 100M-follower accounts.
- Storing full post content in each feed list.
- Treating the feed cache as the source of truth, with no rebuild path.
- Rewriting millions of feed lists on unfollow or delete instead of filtering at read time.
- Sizing the cache for every registered user instead of active users.

## Self-review checklist

- [ ] Posts and follows are durable in sharded stores; the feed is derived and rebuildable.
- [ ] Fan-out on write for normal authors, read-time merge for high-fan-out authors, with a stated threshold.
- [ ] Feed lists hold ids, are capped, and exist only for active users.
- [ ] Hydration is batched and parallel, with over-fetch for filtered items.
- [ ] Pagination uses an opaque cursor, not offsets.
- [ ] Visibility (deletes, blocks, unfollows) is enforced on read.
- [ ] Fan-out lag is monitored against a freshness target, with idempotent writes and backpressure.

## Further reading

- [TAO: Facebook's Distributed Data Store for the Social Graph (USENIX ATC 2013)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc13/technical-sessions/presentation/bronson)
- [Redis documentation: Sorted sets](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/sorted-sets/)
keyTakeaways: Reading about 200 authors for every feed request is too slow at scale. Precompute capped lists of post IDs instead.
Do not push a celebrity's post into millions of lists. Push normal posts ahead of time and merge celebrity posts when someone reads.
Keep IDs, not complete posts, in feed lists. Hydrate from shared post and user caches so edits, deletes and counts stay cheap.
Treat the feed cache as a rebuildable list of candidates, not permission to display them. Re-check visibility on every read.
Page with opaque cursors rather than offsets. For a ranked feed, keep a short-lived session snapshot so the order stays stable while someone scrolls.
